name: teeth
title: How Did Ancient Humans Take Care of Their Teeth?

lines: Imagine waking up with a toothache.
Not a little one. The kind that throbs every time your heart beats.
Now imagine there is no dentist.
No toothbrush. No painkillers.
Nobody even knows what tooth decay is.
So what did ancient humans actually do about their teeth?
Surprisingly, a lot more than you'd think.
And a lot of the evidence is still stuck to their teeth today.
Let's start with the good news.
For most of human history, cavities were actually pretty rare.
Cavities happen when bacteria in your mouth feed on sugars and starches,
and leave behind acid that slowly eats into your teeth.
And for a very long time, people just didn't eat much of that.
Studies of hunter-gatherer teeth usually find decay in somewhere between zero and about fourteen percent of teeth.
But their food came with a different problem.
It was tough, and it was full of grit and sand.
Chewing it day after day slowly wore their teeth down.
So for most of our history, the big problem wasn't holes in teeth.
It was teeth that were worn, chipped and cracked.
And when something got stuck between their teeth?
They did what you might have done after lunch today.
They grabbed a toothpick.
Scientists have found tiny grooves on fossil teeth,
worn in by sticks or grass stems being pushed between the teeth again and again.
Some of these toothpick grooves go back close to two million years,
to early human species like Homo habilis.
But one Neanderthal from Krapina, in what is now Croatia, takes this further.
Around a hundred and thirty thousand years ago, this person had a tooth growing in crooked,
and it was very likely painful.
Their teeth show six toothpick grooves around the problem area, plus scratches and chips.
It looks like they were poking at it, over and over, trying to ease the pain.
It's not dentistry the way we know it.
But it may be one of the earliest signs of someone trying to treat their own toothache.
Then there's a Neanderthal from El Sidrón cave, in Spain.
Scientists took the hardened plaque from this individual's teeth,
and read the ancient DNA trapped inside it.
This Neanderthal had a painful dental abscess.
And in the plaque was DNA from poplar,
a tree that contains salicylic acid, the natural pain reliever behind aspirin.
There were also traces of Penicillium,
the same group of molds that penicillin comes from.
So was this Neanderthal chewing poplar on purpose, to dull the pain?
The researchers say they can't prove it.
But it's hard not to wonder.
Now jump forward to about fourteen thousand years ago,
in the mountains of northern Italy.
A hunter-gatherer buried at a rock shelter called Villabruna
had a large cavity in one of his back molars.
Under a microscope, that cavity is covered in tiny scratches.
They match marks made by a pointed piece of flint,
used to scratch and lever out the rotten part of the tooth, while he was still alive.
No numbing. No drill.
Just a sharp stone, and a lot of courage.
About a thousand years later, someone near Lucca, also in Italy, went a step further.
Two of this person's front teeth had been scraped out,
and the holes were packed with bitumen, a sticky natural tar, mixed with plant fibers and possibly hair.
In other words, it's one of the earliest fillings we know of.
And then, everything changed.
Around ten thousand years ago, people in several parts of the world started farming.
Grains. Porridge. Bread.
Starchy, sticky food, every single day.
Perfect food for the bacteria that cause cavities.
Actually, one group got there early.
At Taforalt, in Morocco, about fifteen thousand years ago, hunter-gatherers ate a lot of acorns.
And almost every adult there had cavities.
More cavities meant more dentistry.
At Mehrgarh, in what is now Pakistan, people who lived around seven and a half to nine thousand years ago
had holes drilled into their molars.
Researchers think the tool was a bow drill tipped with flint.
In tests, a drill like that could cut into tooth enamel in under a minute.
And these holes weren't made after death.
The patients were alive.
Some of them even had more than one tooth drilled.
Then, about sixty-five hundred years ago, in what is now Slovenia,
a man in his twenties had a cracked canine tooth.
Someone filled the crack with beeswax.
It may have been to stop the pain when he chewed.
Although scientists can't completely rule out that the wax was added after he died.
So, did ancient humans take care of their teeth?
Not the way we do. No brushing twice a day. No floss. No checkups.
But they picked at them, scraped out the rot with stone,
drilled with flint, and plugged the holes with tar and wax.
And the strangest part?
Their biggest tooth problem came from the very thing that made modern life possible.
Farming.
So next time you're sitting in a dentist's chair, remember.
It could be a lot worse.
It could be a sharp rock.
Follow for more of how it really works.
